nodes.label: Median history from Herodotus alone
nodes.full: Unlike Elam, Babylon or Assyria, the Medes left no substantial inscriptions or archives of their own, so nearly everything known about internal Median politics comes from Herodotus, writing more than a century after Astyages's fall — a single external, narratively shaped source that historians can corroborate only at the handful of points, like the fall of Nineveh, where a Babylonian record happens to survive.
nodes.src: Herodotus, Histories, book 1; the near-total absence of a native Median textual record.

nodes.label: Deioces founds Media
nodes.full: Herodotus credits Deioces with uniting the Median tribes and founding Ecbatana as a fortified royal seat, elected by his own people for his reputation as a just arbiter of disputes — a foundation story that reads as much like a moral parable about the origins of kingship as a documented political event, and most modern historians treat its details with real caution.
nodes.src: Herodotus, Histories 1.96–101 (the sole detailed source for Deioces).

nodes.label: Magi as a Median tribe
nodes.full: Herodotus explicitly lists the Magi among the six tribes making up the Median people, distinct from the ruling tribe itself — the earliest identification of the priestly caste that would go on to serve every Iranian dynasty from the Medes through the Achaemenids and beyond as ritual specialists and interpreters of royal dreams.
nodes.src: Herodotus, Histories 1.101.

nodes.label: Ecbatana’s seven walls
nodes.full: Herodotus describes Ecbatana as ringed by seven concentric walls of increasing height, each painted a different colour, with the innermost plated in silver and gold — a vivid architectural description that has never been archaeologically confirmed, since the ancient site lies directly beneath the modern city of Hamadan and has never been fully excavated.
nodes.src: Herodotus, Histories 1.98, flagged as unverified by excavation.

nodes.label: Phraortes and the Scythians
nodes.full: Phraortes extended Median rule over neighbouring Iranian peoples before dying in battle against Assyria; Herodotus's account of a subsequent 28-year period of Scythian overlordship, ended by a mass killing of drunken Scythian chieftains at a banquet, cannot be independently confirmed but would place Media under steppe domination for over a generation.
nodes.src: Herodotus, Histories 1.102–106.

nodes.label: Phraortes dies fighting Assyria
nodes.full: Phraortes died campaigning against the Assyrian Empire at the height of its own power under Ashurbanipal — a defeat that nonetheless demonstrated Median ambitions had grown large enough to challenge Assyria directly, decades before Cyaxares would finish what Phraortes began.
nodes.src: Herodotus, Histories 1.102.

nodes.label: Scythian domination
nodes.full: According to Herodotus, Scythian raiders who had originally been invited in to help fight Assyria instead imposed their own domination over Media for nearly three decades, ended only when Cyaxares had a large number of Scythian chieftains killed at a banquet after getting them deliberately drunk.
nodes.src: Herodotus, Histories 1.106.

nodes.label: Highland economy
nodes.full: The Zagros highlands' pastoral and agricultural economy, combined with control of the horse-breeding pastures the region was already famous for in antiquity, gave Media the cavalry and logistical base that let Cyaxares field an army capable of destroying an empire as large as Assyria's.
nodes.src: Herodotus, Histories 3.106, on the region's celebrated horse pastures (referring to the later Nisaean plain tradition).

nodes.label: Army reorganised
nodes.full: Herodotus credits Cyaxares with the first organisation of Median forces into distinct units of spearmen, archers and cavalry, replacing an earlier undifferentiated levy — a military reform that, whether or not the specific details are reliable, plausibly underlies the army's evident new effectiveness against both the Scythians and Assyria.
nodes.src: Herodotus, Histories 1.103.

nodes.label: Roads from Ecbatana
nodes.full: Some connected road network linking Ecbatana to the wider plateau almost certainly predated the famous Achaemenid Royal Road, since Cyaxares's campaigns against Assyria and the later Median-Persian transition both required rapid, organised troop movement across considerable distances — infrastructure Darius I's later road more likely formalised and extended than invented outright.
nodes.src: Inferred from Median campaign logistics; no directly dated Median-era road remains have been identified with certainty.

nodes.label: Cyaxares
nodes.full: Cyaxares reorganised the Median army, threw off Scythian domination, and allied with Nabopolassar of Babylon to destroy the Assyrian Empire outright — the most consequential and best independently corroborated reign of the whole Median dynasty, its central act changing the political map of the entire Near East.
nodes.src: Herodotus, Histories 1.103–106; the Babylonian Chronicle (Fall of Nineveh Chronicle), corroborating the Median-Babylonian alliance.

nodes.label: Fall of Nineveh
nodes.full: A combined Median and Babylonian army stormed and utterly destroyed Nineveh, the Assyrian capital, ending an empire that had dominated the Near East for centuries — the Babylonian Chronicle's own account of the siege corroborates Herodotus in its broad outline, one of the rare points where Median history touches an independent contemporary record.
nodes.src: The Fall of Nineveh Chronicle (Babylonian Chronicle series); Herodotus, Histories 1.106.

nodes.label: Assyria’s fall reshapes the Near East
nodes.full: Assyria's destruction left a power vacuum the victors and their neighbours divided among themselves into a new system of four major kingdoms — Media in the north and east, a revived Babylon in the south, Lydia in Anatolia, and Egypt to the west — a geopolitical arrangement that would last only a couple of generations before Cyrus began absorbing it piece by piece.
nodes.src: Comparative Near Eastern political history following the fall of Nineveh.

nodes.label: Marriage alliance with Babylon
nodes.full: Cyaxares's daughter (or granddaughter, in some readings of the sources) Amytis married the Babylonian crown prince Nebuchadnezzar, sealing the Median-Babylonian alliance with a dynastic tie — later Greek tradition would even attribute Babylon's legendary Hanging Gardens to Nebuchadnezzar's wish to ease his highland-born wife's homesickness for Media's mountains.
nodes.src: Berossus, Babyloniaca (via Josephus), on Amytis and the tradition of the Hanging Gardens.

nodes.label: Battle of the Eclipse
nodes.full: A solar eclipse — reportedly predicted in advance by the philosopher Thales — interrupted a pitched battle between Median and Lydian armies on the Halys river so dramatically that both sides broke off fighting and negotiated an immediate peace, sealed by a royal marriage alliance between the two dynasties.
nodes.src: Herodotus, Histories 1.74.

nodes.label: Marriage alliance with Lydia
nodes.full: The peace ending the Battle of the Eclipse was sealed by the marriage of Astyages to Aryenis, daughter of the Lydian king Alyattes — a diplomatic marriage fixing the Halys river as the recognised frontier between the Median and Lydian spheres for the remainder of both kingdoms' independent existence.
nodes.src: Herodotus, Histories 1.74.

nodes.label: Astyages
nodes.full: Astyages ruled the Median kingdom at its greatest territorial extent before his own grandson Cyrus, king of the vassal Persians, rose in revolt and overthrew him in 550 BC — an ending Herodotus frames around a dream-omen and the infant Cyrus's legendary exposure, but whose basic outcome, the transfer of Iranian overlordship from Ecbatana to Persis, is not in doubt.
nodes.src: Herodotus, Histories 1.107–130; Nabonidus Chronicle, corroborating Cyrus's revolt against Astyages.

nodes.label: Media at its height
nodes.full: Under Astyages, Median overlordship extended from the Halys river in Anatolia across the Iranian plateau, making it — on paper — one of the largest and most powerful states in the Near East on the very eve of its sudden collapse to a vassal king's revolt.
nodes.src: Herodotus, Histories 1.103, 1.130, on the extent of Median rule before Cyrus's revolt.

nodes.label: Legend of the infant Cyrus
nodes.full: Herodotus frames Astyages's fall around a dream that his daughter Mandane's son would overthrow him, the infant Cyrus's ordered exposure, and his survival and secret upbringing by a herdsman — a foundation legend following a pattern common to many cultures' origin stories for a future conqueror, which historians read as testifying to later Persian mythmaking about Cyrus more than to verifiable events at the Median court.
nodes.src: Herodotus, Histories 1.107–122, explicitly flagged by Herodotus himself as one of several competing versions he had heard.

nodes.label: Cyrus’s revolt
nodes.full: Cyrus, king of the Persian vassal state, rose against his grandfather Astyages; part of the Median army defected to him under the general Harpagus, and Astyages's own capital Ecbatana fell to Cyrus in 550 BC — the event that ended Median supremacy and began the Achaemenid Persian Empire in the very same stroke.
nodes.src: Nabonidus Chronicle, on Cyrus's victory over Astyages; Herodotus, Histories 1.123–130.
